nodes.name: Functional linear regression model
nodes.statement: Most work in this area involves different approaches for fitting the functional linear regression model, \begin{equation} Y_i = \int\beta(t) X_i(t) \,dt + \varepsilon_i, \qquad i = 1,\ldots, n. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Functional linear regression model equation
nodes.statement: Y_i = \int\beta(t) X_i(t) \,dt + \varepsilon_i, \qquad i = 1,\ldots, n.
nodes.label: flin

nodes.name: Centered response and predictors
nodes.statement: For notational convenience, we assume throughout this paper that the response and predictors have been centered so the intercept can be ignored.

nodes.name: Functional additive regression framework
nodes.statement: In this paper, we address both of these limitations using a functional additive regression framework of the form \begin{equation} Y_i = \sum_{j=1}^p f_j (X_{ij} )+ \varepsilon_i, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, n, \end{equation} where the $f_j$'s are general nonlinear functions of $X_{ij}(t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Additive model $Y_i=\sum_j f_j(X_{ij})+\varepsilon_i$ with nonlinear functions of functional predictors.

nodes.name: Functional additive model equation
nodes.statement: Y_i = \sum_{j=1}^p f_j (X_{ij} )+ \varepsilon_i, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, n,
nodes.label: far

nodes.name: Functional Additive Regression (FAR)
nodes.statement: In this paper, we suggest a new penalized least squares method called \emph{Functional Additive Regression}, or FAR, for fitting a nonlinear functional additive model.
differentia: for fitting a nonlinear functional additive model
also_stated_at: We suggest a new method, called \textit{Functional Additive Regression}, or FAR, for efficiently performing high-dimensional functional regression.

nodes.name: Vector of component values f_j
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathbf f}_j= (f_j(X_{1j}),\ldots,f_j(X_{nj}) )^T$.

nodes.name: General FAR penalized regression criterion
nodes.statement: Then our general approach for fitting (\ref{far}) is to minimize the following penalized regression criterion over ${\mathbf f}_1, {\mathbf f}_2,\ldots, {\mathbf f}_p$: \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2n} \Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}-\sum _{j=1}^p {\mathbf f}_j \Biggr\Vert ^2_2 + \sum_{j=1}^p \rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}{\Vert{\mathbf f}_j\Vert }_2 \biggr), \end{equation} where ${\mathbf Y}=(Y_1,\ldots, Y_n)^T$, $\rho_{\lambda_n}(t)$ is a penalty function, $\lambda_n$ is the regularization parameter and ${\Vert {\mathbf f}_j\Vert }_2=\sqrt{{\mathbf f}_j^T{\mathbf f}_j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize penalized least squares $\frac{1}{2n}\|Y-\sum_j f_j\|^2+\sum_j\rho_{\lambda_n}(\|f_j\|/\sqrt n)$ over the component vectors.

nodes.name: FAR criterion (fundamental)
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{2n} \Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}-\sum _{j=1}^p {\mathbf f}_j \Biggr\Vert ^2_2 + \sum_{j=1}^p \rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}{\Vert{\mathbf f}_j\Vert }_2 \biggr),
nodes.label: fundamental

nodes.name: l2 norm notation
nodes.statement: To aid the presentation, we drop the subscript and use $\Vert \cdot\Vert $ to denote the $\ell_2$ norm of a vector in the future.

nodes.name: Fully observed trajectories
nodes.statement: We assume that the trajectories of functional predictors, $X_{ij}(t)$, are fully observed.

nodes.name: Single index model
nodes.statement: For a centered response, the standard single index model can be expressed in the form $Y=g({\bolds\beta}^T{\mathbf X}) + \varepsilon$, where $g(x)$ is a general nonlinear function and ${\bolds\beta}$ is a norm one vector representing the best single direction to project the predictors into.
nodes.statement_short: $Y=g(\beta^TX)+\varepsilon$ with nonlinear link $g$ and unit direction $\beta$.

nodes.name: Functional single index model
nodes.statement: Index models can be naturally extended to functional predictors using the formulation $f_j(X_{ij}) = g_j (\int\beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt )$, where $g_j(x)$ and $\beta_j(t)$ are both nonparametric smooth functions, and the integral is well-defined.
nodes.origin_citation: James & Silverman; Amato et al.; Ait-Saidi et al.; Chen et al.; Ferraty et al.
nodes.statement_short: $f_j(X_{ij})=g_j(\int\beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)dt)$ with smooth link $g_j$ and index function $\beta_j$.

nodes.name: FAR single index model
nodes.statement: Y_i = \sum_{j=1}^p g_j \biggl(\int\beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt \biggr) + \varepsilon_i.
nodes.label: simfar

nodes.name: Centered regression functions
nodes.statement: For identifiability, in addition to centering the response, we also center the regression functions: $\sum_{i=1}^n g_j (\int\beta _j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt )=0$ for all~$j$.

nodes.name: Nonlinear FAR optimization criterion
nodes.statement: The general FAR optimization criterion~(\ref{fundamental}) becomes \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2n} \Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}-\sum _{j=1}^p g_j \biggl(\int \beta_j(t) {\mathbf X}_j(t)\,dt \biggr)\Biggr\Vert ^2 + \sum_{j=1}^p \rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl(\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\Vert{\mathbf f}_j\Vert \biggr), \end{equation} where\vspace*{1pt} ${\mathbf X}_j(t) = (X_{1j}(t), \ldots, X_{nj}(t))^T$ and $g_j (\int\beta_j(t) {\mathbf X}_j(t)\,dt ) = (f_j(X_{1j}), \ldots,\break f_j(X_{nj}))^T$.
nodes.statement_short: FAR criterion with single-index components $g_j(\int\beta_j X_j)$.

nodes.name: Nonlinear FAR criterion (nonlinfar)
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{2n} \Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}-\sum _{j=1}^p g_j \biggl(\int \beta_j(t) {\mathbf X}_j(t)\,dt \biggr)\Biggr\Vert ^2 + \sum_{j=1}^p \rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl(\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\Vert{\mathbf f}_j\Vert \biggr),
nodes.label: nonlinfar

nodes.name: Observation range [0,1]
nodes.statement: We assume without loss of generality that each predictor is observed over the range $0\le t \le1$.

nodes.name: Linear FAR optimization criterion
nodes.statement: Hence, in the linear setting, \begin{equation} f_j(X_{ij}) = \int_0^1 \beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt, \end{equation} where $\beta_j(t)$ is an unknown smooth coefficient function, and the FAR optimization criterion becomes \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2n} \Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}-\sum _{j=1}^p \int_0^1 \beta_j(t) {\mathbf X}_j(t)\,dt\Biggr\Vert^2 + \sum_{j=1}^p \rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl( \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Vert{\mathbf f}_j\Vert\biggr), \end{equation} where ${\mathbf X}_j(t)= (X_{1j}(t),\ldots,X_{nj}(t) )^T$.
nodes.statement_short: FAR criterion with linear components $f_j(X_{ij})=\int_0^1\beta_j X_{ij}$.

nodes.name: Linear component
nodes.statement: f_j(X_{ij}) = \int_0^1 \beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt,
nodes.label: linearf

nodes.name: Linear FAR criterion (linearfar)
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{2n} \Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}-\sum _{j=1}^p \int_0^1 \beta_j(t) {\mathbf X}_j(t)\,dt\Biggr\Vert^2 + \sum_{j=1}^p \rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl( \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Vert{\mathbf f}_j\Vert\biggr),
nodes.label: linearfar

nodes.name: Orthonormal basis expansion of predictors and coefficients
nodes.statement: Given an orthonormal basis $\{b_{l}(t)\}$, the functional predictors and the corresponding regression coefficients can be decomposed as \begin{equation} X_{ij}(t) = \sum_{l=1}^\infty \theta_{ijl}b_l(t), \qquad\beta_j(t) = \sum _{l=1}^\infty\eta_{0,jl}b_l(t), \end{equation} where $\theta_{ijl}$ and $\eta_{0,jl}$ are the coefficients of $X_{ij}(t)$ and $\beta_j(t)$ corresponding to the $l$th basis function $b_l(t)$, respectively.

nodes.name: Basis representation
nodes.statement: X_{ij}(t) = \sum_{l=1}^\infty \theta_{ijl}b_l(t), \qquad\beta_j(t) = \sum _{l=1}^\infty\eta_{0,jl}b_l(t),
nodes.label: eqbasis-rep

nodes.name: Basis expansion of additive component
nodes.statement: f_j(X_{ij}) = \int_0^1 X_{ij}(t)\beta_j(t)\,dt = \sum_{l=1}^\infty \theta_{ijl}\eta_{0,jl}.
nodes.label: fexpan

nodes.name: Truncation level q_n and truncated coefficient vectors
nodes.statement: Specifically, for a given sequence of integers $q_n = o(n)$ depending only on the sample size $n$, write $\bolds\eta_{0j} = (\eta_{0,j1},\ldots ,\eta_{0,jq_n})^T$ and $\bolds\theta_{ij} = (\theta_{ij1},\ldots, \theta _{ijq_n})^T$.

nodes.name: Approximation error e_ij
nodes.statement: Denote by $e_{ij}$ the approximation error, that is, \begin{equation} e_{ij} = f_j(X_{ij})- \bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_{0j} = \sum _{l=q_n+1}^\infty\theta_{ijl}\eta_{0,jl}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Approximation error definition
nodes.statement: e_{ij} = f_j(X_{ij})- \bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_{0j} = \sum _{l=q_n+1}^\infty\theta_{ijl}\eta_{0,jl}.
nodes.label: deferr

nodes.name: Uniform bound on basis approximation error
nodes.statement: Then by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality and Condition~\ref{as3} in Appendix~\ref{appb}, uniformly across all $i = 1,\ldots, n$ and $j\in \mathfrak{M}_0$, \begin{eqnarray} \qquad\vert e_{ij}\vert^2& \leq&\sum _{l=q_n+1}^\infty\eta_{0,jl}^2l^{-4} \sum_{l=q_n+1}^\infty\theta_{ijl}^2l^{4} \leq C^2 q_n^{-4}\sum _{l=q_n+1}^\infty\eta_{0,jl}^2 \leq \widetilde C C^2q_n^{-4}, \end{eqnarray} where $C$ and $\widetilde C$ are two positive constants defined in Condition~\ref{as3}.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz with the Sobolev condition gives $|e_{ij}|^2\le \widetilde C C^2 q_n^{-4}$.

nodes.name: Approximation error bound
nodes.statement: \qquad\vert e_{ij}\vert^2& \leq&\sum _{l=q_n+1}^\infty\eta_{0,jl}^2l^{-4} \sum_{l=q_n+1}^\infty\theta_{ijl}^2l^{4} \leq C^2 q_n^{-4}\sum _{l=q_n+1}^\infty\eta_{0,jl}^2 \leq \widetilde C C^2q_n^{-4},
nodes.label: eqapp-err

nodes.name: Basis coefficient matrix Theta_j
nodes.statement: Let $\Theta_j$ be an $n\times q_n$ matrix whose rows are formed by $\{\bolds\theta_{ij}, i=1,\ldots, n\}$.

nodes.name: Truncated linear FAR criterion
nodes.statement: Then, if $q_n$ is large enough, $f_j(X_{ij})\approx \bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_{0j}$ and (\ref{linearfar}) can be approximated by \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2n}\Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}- \sum _{j=1}^p\Theta_j\bolds\eta_j \Biggr\Vert^2+\sum_{j=1}^p \rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Vert\Theta_j \bolds\eta_j\Vert\biggr). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Group-penalized least squares over basis coefficients $\eta_j$ approximating the linear FAR criterion.

nodes.name: Truncated FAR criterion (newopt2)
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{2n}\Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}- \sum _{j=1}^p\Theta_j\bolds\eta_j \Biggr\Vert^2+\sum_{j=1}^p \rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Vert\Theta_j \bolds\eta_j\Vert\biggr).
nodes.label: newopt2

nodes.name: Closed-form group-lasso coordinate update
nodes.statement: If $\rho_{\lambda_n}(t) = \lambda_nt$, then the solution to (\ref {newopt2}) satisfies $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j = \Theta_j\hat{\bolds\eta}_j$ where \[ \hat{\bolds\eta}_j = \biggl(1-\frac{\sqrt{n}\lambda_n}{\Vert S_j{\mathbf R}_j\Vert } \biggr)_+\bigl( \Theta_j^T \Theta_j\bigr)^{-1} \Theta_j^T{\mathbf R}_j, \] $S_j = \Theta_j(\Theta_j^T\Theta_j)^{-1}\Theta_j^T$, ${\mathbf R}_j = {\mathbf Y} - \sum_{k\neq j}\Theta_k\hat{\bolds\eta}_k$, and $z_+ = \max(0,z)$ represents the positive part of $z$.
nodes.statement_short: With the lasso penalty, each block minimizer is a shrunken projection of the partial residual onto $\Theta_j$.
nodes.label: propL1

nodes.name: Linear FAR algorithm
nodes.statement: \caption{\textbf{Linear FAR algorithm}} \begin{enumerate} \item[0.] Initialize~$\hat{\bolds\eta}_j={\mathbf0}$ and $S_j=\Theta _j (\Theta_j^T\Theta_j )^{-1} \Theta_j^T$, for $j\in\{ 1,\ldots,p\}$. \item[1.] Fix all $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_k$ for $k\ne j$. Compute the residual vector ${\mathbf R}_j = {\mathbf Y}- \sum_{k\ne j} \hat{{\mathbf f}}_k$. \item[2.] Let $\widehat{\mathbf P}_j = S_j {\mathbf R}_j$ represent the unshrunk estimate for ${\mathbf f}_j$.\vspace*{2pt} \item[3.] Let $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j = \alpha_j \widehat{\mathbf P}_j$ where $\alpha_j = (1-\lambda_n\sqrt n/\Vert \widehat{\mathbf P}_j\Vert )_+$ is a shrinkage parameter.\vspace*{3pt} \item[4.] Center $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j \leftarrow\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j - \operatorname{mean}(\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j)$.\vspace*{2pt} \item[5.] Repeat steps~1 through 4 for $j=1,2,\ldots, p$ and iterate until convergence. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Block coordinate descent: project partial residuals onto each predictor's basis, then apply group soft-threshold shrinkage.
nodes.label: alglin

nodes.statement: [4.] Center $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j \leftarrow\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j - \operatorname{mean}(\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j)$.\vspace*{2pt}

nodes.name: Cycle over predictors until convergence
nodes.statement:
[5.] Repeat steps~1 through 4 for $j=1,2,\ldots, p$ and iterate until
convergence.

nodes.name: Monotone decrease of the criterion
nodes.statement: In addition, it is clear from Proposition~\ref{propL1} that (\ref{newopt2}) will decrease at each step.

nodes.name: Local linear approximation for general penalties
nodes.statement: For a general penalty function, $\rho_{\lambda_n}(t)$, we use the local linear approximation method proposed in \cite{ZL08} to solve (\ref{newopt2}). The penalty function can be approximated as $\rho _{\lambda_n}(\Vert {\mathbf f}\Vert /\sqrt n)\approx \rho'_{\lambda_n}(\Vert {\mathbf f}^*\Vert /\sqrt n)\Vert {\mathbf f} \Vert /\sqrt n+C$, where ${\mathbf f}^*$ is some vector that is close to ${\mathbf f}$ and $C=\rho_{\lambda _n}(\Vert {\mathbf f}^*\Vert /\sqrt n)-\rho_{\lambda_n}'(\Vert {\mathbf f}^*\Vert /\sqrt n)\Vert {\mathbf f} ^*\Vert /\sqrt n$ is a constant. Hence, the only required change to the FAR algorithm for optimizing over general penalty functions is to replace the calculation of $\alpha_j$ in step~3 by \[ \alpha_j = \biggl(1-\rho'_{\lambda_n}\biggl( \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Vert\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j\Vert\biggr)\sqrt n/\Vert\widehat {\mathbf P}_j\Vert\biggr)_+, \] where $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j$ represents the most recent estimate for ${\mathbf f}_j$. The initial estimate of $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j$ can be obtained by using the Lasso penalty. This simple approximation allows the FAR algorithm to be easily applied to a wide range of penalty functions.
nodes.statement_short: General concave penalties handled by local linear approximation, changing only the shrinkage factor in step 3.

nodes.name: Basis approximation of link functions
nodes.statement: We assume that $g_j(x)$ can be well approximated by a $d_n$-dimensional basis ${\mathbf h}(x)$ such that $g_j(x) \approx {\mathbf h}(x)^T \bolds\xi_j$.

nodes.name: Nonlinear FAR criterion in basis form
nodes.statement: Using this basis, representation (\ref{nonlinfar}) can be expressed as \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2n} \Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}-\sum _{j=1}^p H_j\bolds\xi_j\Biggr \Vert^2 + \sum_{j=1}^p \rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl(\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\Vert H_j \bolds\xi_j\Vert\biggr), \end{equation} where\vspace*{2pt} $H_j$ is an $n$ by $d_n$ matrix who's $i$th row is given by ${\mathbf h}(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T \bolds\eta_j )^T$.
nodes.statement_short: Group-penalized least squares over link coefficients $\xi_j$ with design $H_j$ built from the index $\theta_{ij}^T\eta_j$.

nodes.name: Nonlinear FAR criterion (nonlinfar2)
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{2n} \Biggl\Vert{\mathbf Y}-\sum _{j=1}^p H_j\bolds\xi_j\Biggr \Vert^2 + \sum_{j=1}^p \rho_{\lambda_n} \biggl(\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\Vert H_j \bolds\xi_j\Vert\biggr),
nodes.label: nonlinfar2

nodes.name: Index sum of squares (etaopt)
nodes.statement: \sum_{i=1}^n \Biggl(Y_i-\sum_{j=1}^p{\mathbf h} \bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T \bolds\eta_j \bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j \Biggr)^2
nodes.label: etaopt

nodes.name: Nonlinear FAR algorithm
nodes.statement: \caption{\textbf{Nonlinear FAR algorithm}} \begin{enumerate} \item[0.] Initialize\vspace*{2pt}~$\hat{\bolds\eta}_j$ for $j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$ using the linear FAR algorithm. \item[1.] Compute $\widehat H_j$ using the current estimates for $\bolds\eta_j$. \item[2.] Estimate $\bolds\xi_j$ for $j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$ by minimizing (\ref{nonlinfar2}) given the current values of $\widehat H_j$. \item[3.] Conditional on the $\hat{\bolds\xi}_j$'s from step~2, estimate the $\bolds\eta_j$'s by minimizing (\ref{etaopt}). \item[4.] Repeat steps 1~through 3 and iterate until convergence. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Alternate between fitting link coefficients by linear FAR and re-estimating index directions by least squares.
nodes.label: algnonlin

nodes.name: Initialize indices by linear FAR
nodes.statement:
[0.] Initialize\vspace*{2pt}~$\hat{\bolds\eta}_j$ for $j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$
using the linear FAR algorithm.

nodes.name: Compute design H_j
nodes.statement: [1.] Compute $\widehat H_j$ using the current estimates for $\bolds\eta_j$.

nodes.name: Fit link coefficients
nodes.statement:
[2.] Estimate $\bolds\xi_j$ for $j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}$ by minimizing
(\ref{nonlinfar2}) given the current values of $\widehat H_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the penalized problem (nonlinfar2) for $\xi_j$ with $H_j$ fixed.

nodes.name: Re-estimate index vectors
nodes.statement:
[3.] Conditional on the $\hat{\bolds\xi}_j$'s from step~2, estimate the
$\bolds\eta_j$'s by minimizing (\ref{etaopt}).
nodes.statement_short: Least squares in $\eta_j$ given the fitted links.

nodes.name: Iterate until convergence
nodes.statement: [4.] Repeat steps 1~through 3 and iterate until convergence.

nodes.name: Link-coefficient step reduces to linear FAR
nodes.statement: One of the appealing aspects of this approach is that, for fixed $\widehat H_j$, (\ref{newopt2}) and (\ref{nonlinfar2}) are equivalent so estimation of the $\bolds\xi_j$'s in step 2 can be achieved using the linear FAR algorithm from Section~\ref{seclinearfar}.

nodes.name: True predictor set M_0 and sparsity s_n
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathfrak{M}_0 = \{j: \beta_j(t)\neq0, 1\leq j\leq p\}$ the set of true functional predictors and let $s_n$ represent the cardinality of $\mathfrak{M}_0$.

nodes.name: True coefficient vector eta_0
nodes.statement: Let $\bolds\eta_0 = (\bolds\eta_{0,1}, \ldots, \bolds\eta_{0,p}) \in R^{pq_n}$ with $\bolds\eta _{0j}$ representing the true coefficient vector in the basis representation $f_j(X_{ij}) = \bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_{0j} + e_{ij}$.

nodes.name: Stacked vectors and matrices over an index set
nodes.statement: For\vspace*{1pt} any index set $S \subset\{1,\ldots, p\}$, we use $\bolds\eta_S$ to denote the vector formed by stacking vectors $\bolds\eta_j$, $j\in S$ one underneath each other, and $\Theta_S$ to denote the matrix formed by stacking the matrices $\Theta_j$, $j\in S$ one after another.

nodes.name: Column standardization of Theta
nodes.statement: Moreover, we standardize each column of $\Theta$ such that they all have $\ell_2$-norm $\sqrt{n}$.

nodes.name: Oracle model selection property of linear FAR
nodes.statement: Assume that $q_n + \log p = O(n\lambda_n^2) $, $\lambda_n n^{\alpha}q_n\sqrt{s_n} \rightarrow0$, and $\log (pq_n) = o(n^{1-2\alpha}s_n^{-1}q_n^{-2})$ with $\alpha$ defined in Condition~\ref{as2}\textup{(B)}. Further assume that $s_nq_n^{-2} = o(\lambda _n)$, then under Conditions~\ref{as3} and~\ref{as2}, with probability tending to 1 as $ n \rightarrow\infty$, there exists a local minimizer $\hat{\bolds\eta}$ of (\ref{newopt2}) such that: \begin{longlist}[(2)] \item[(1)] $\hat{\bolds\eta}_{\mathfrak{M}_0^c}=0$, \item[(2)] $\Vert \hat{\bolds\eta}_{\mathfrak{M}_0} - \bolds\eta_{0\mathfrak{M}_0}\Vert _\infty\leq c_0^{1/2}n^{-\alpha}q_n^{-1/2}$, \end{longlist} where $\Vert \cdot\Vert _\infty$ stands for the infinity norm of a vector.
nodes.statement_short: With probability tending to 1 a local minimizer of the linear FAR criterion zeroes all noise predictors and estimates signal coefficients at sup-norm rate $n^{-\alpha}q_n^{-1/2}$.
nodes.label: T2

nodes.name: Local minimizers lie within statistical precision (Loh-Wainwright)
nodes.statement: Although Theorem~\ref{T2} is on a local minimizer of the linear FAR criterion (\ref{newopt2}), it has been proved by \cite{loh13} that any local minimizer will fall within statistical precision of the true parameter vector under appropriate conditions on the penalty function.
conclusions: any local minimizer will fall within statistical precision of the true parameter vector

nodes.name: Estimated and true component vectors
nodes.statement: Denote by $\hat{\mathbf f}_j = \Theta_j\hat{\bolds\eta}_j$ and ${\mathbf f}_{0j} = (f_j(X_{j1}), \ldots, f_j(X_{jn}))^T$, respectively, the estimated and true values of the $j$th functional component, both evaluated at the $n$ training data points.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1
nodes.statement: Then the corollary below follows immediately from Theorem~\ref{T2} and Condition~\ref{as3}.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from Theorem 1 combined with the basis approximation condition.

nodes.name: Selection consistency and error bound for FAR component estimates
nodes.statement: Suppose the conditions in Theorem~\ref {T2} are satisfied. Then with probability tending to 1 as $n\rightarrow \infty$, there exists a FAR estimate such that $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j = 0$ for $j\notin\mathfrak{M}_0$, and \[ \max_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Vert\hat{{\mathbf f}}_j - {\mathbf f}_{0j}\Vert_2 \leq C_2n^{-\alpha}, \] where $C_2$ is some positive constant.
assumptions: Suppose the conditions in Theorem~\ref {T2} are satisfied.
nodes.label: cor1

nodes.name: Asymptotic normality of linear FAR estimator
nodes.statement: Assume that the conditions in Theorem~\ref{T2} hold and in addition, $\rho_{\lambda_n}'(a_n/2)=o(a_nn^{\alpha-\sfrac{1}{2}}s_n^{-1/2})$, $\sup_{t\geq\sfrac{a_n}{2}}\rho_{\lambda_n}''(t)=O(n^{-1/2})$, $s_{n}=o(n^{2\alpha})$ and $s_nq_n^{-2} = o(n^{-1/2})$. Then with probability tending to 1 as $n \rightarrow\infty$, there exists a strict local minimizer $\hat{\bolds\eta}$ of (\ref{newopt2}) such that $\hat{\bolds\eta}_{\mathfrak{M}_0^c} = 0$ and \[ {\mathbf c}^T \bigl[\bigl(\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^T \Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}\bigr)^{1/2}(\hat{\bolds\eta}_{\mathfrak{M}_0} - \bolds\eta_{0,\mathfrak{M}_0}) + n\bigl(\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^T\Theta _{\mathfrak{M}_0}\bigr)^{-1/2}{\mathbf v}_{0,\mathfrak{M}_0}\bigr] \stackrel{\mathscr{D}}{\longrightarrow} N\bigl(0, \sigma^2\bigr), \] where ${\mathbf c}\in\mathbf{R}^{q_ns_n}$ satisfies ${\mathbf c}^T{\mathbf c}= 1$ and ${\mathbf v}_{0,\mathfrak{M}_0}$ is a vector formed by stacking the vectors ${\mathbf v}_{0,k}=\rho'_{\lambda_n}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Vert \Theta_k \bolds\eta _{0,k}\Vert )\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \frac{\Theta_k^T\Theta_k\bolds\eta _{0,k}}{\Vert \Theta_k\bolds\eta_{0,k}\Vert }$, $k\in\mathfrak{M}_0$ underneath each other.
conclusions: there exists a strict local minimizer $\hat{\bolds\eta}$ of (\ref{newopt2}) such that $\hat{\bolds\eta}_{\mathfrak{M}_0^c} = 0$
nodes.statement_short: A strict local minimizer has zero noise coefficients and, after bias correction, asymptotically normal projections of signal coefficients.
nodes.label: T3

nodes.name: Projected true and estimated values at a new observation
nodes.statement: Let $f_{0j}^* = {\bolds\theta_j^*}^T\bolds\eta_{0j}$ and $\hat f_{j}^* = {\bolds\theta^*_j}^T\hat{\bolds\eta}_{j}$, with $\bolds\theta_j^*\in R^{q_n}$ the coefficient vector when projecting a given new observation, $X^*_j(t)$, onto the basis function, $\mathbf{b}(t)$.

nodes.name: Stacked vectors f_0^* and hat f^*
nodes.statement: Define ${\mathbf f}_0^* = (f_{01}^*, \ldots, f_{0p}^*)^T$ and $\hat{{\mathbf f}}^* = (\hat f_1^*, \ldots, \hat f_p^*)^T$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2
nodes.statement: Taking ${\mathbf c}= (\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^T\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0})^{-1/2}\Theta^*\tilde{\mathbf c} _0$ with $\Theta^* = \operatorname{diag} ({\bolds\theta_1^*}, \ldots, {\bolds\theta_{s_n}^*} )\in R^{(q_ns_n) \times s_n}$ in Theorem~\ref{T3} and $\tilde{\mathbf c}_0$ a vector in $R^{s_n}$, we have the following asymptotic normality of ${\mathbf f}_0^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 2 with a specific choice of the contrast vector $\mathbf c$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic normality of FAR predictions at a new observation
nodes.statement: Assume that the conditions in Theorem~\ref{T3} hold. Then with probability tending to 1 as $n \rightarrow\infty$, there exists a FAR estimate such that $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_{\mathfrak{M}_0^c}^* = 0$. Moreover, \[ \tilde{\mathbf c}^T_0\bigl[\hat{{\mathbf f}}_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^* - {\mathbf f}_{0,\mathfrak{M}_0}^* + n\bigl(\Theta^*\bigr)^T\bigl( \Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^T\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}\bigr)^{-1} {\mathbf v}_{0,\mathfrak{M} _0}\bigr]\stackrel{\mathscr{D}}{\longrightarrow} N\bigl(0, \sigma^2\bigr), \] where $\tilde{\mathbf c}_0$ is a vector in $R^{s_n}$ satisfying $\tilde{\mathbf c} _0^T(\Theta^*)^T(\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^T\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0})^{-1}\Theta ^*\tilde{\mathbf c}_0 = 1$, and ${\mathbf v}_{0,\mathfrak{M}_0}$ is defined in Theorem~\ref{T3}.
assumptions: Assume that the conditions in Theorem~\ref{T3} hold.
conclusions: there exists a FAR estimate such that $\hat{{\mathbf f}}_{\mathfrak{M}_0^c}^* = 0$

nodes.name: Deterministic predictors
nodes.statement: We treat all the predictors as deterministic.

nodes.name: Centered true regression functions and response
nodes.statement: For identifiability purposes, we assume that the true regression functions, $f_{0j}$, as well as the response vector, are centered, that is, $\sum_{i=1}^n f_{0j}(X_{ij})=0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i=0$.

nodes.name: Cubic B-spline approximation of link functions
nodes.statement: We use cubic B-splines to approximate the true ``link'' functions, $g_{0j}$.

nodes.name: B-spline basis for candidate link function
nodes.statement: Given a candidate index vector $\bolds\eta_j$, the B-spline basis for representing a candidate link function for the $j$th predictor is constructed using uniformly placed knots on the interval $[\min_i \bolds\eta^T_j\bolds\theta_{ij},\max_i \bolds\eta^T_j\bolds\theta_{ij}]$. The corresponding row vector valued basis function is denoted by~${\mathbf h} _{\bolds\eta_j,j}$.

nodes.name: Class of candidate regression functions F_j^0
nodes.statement: We denote by ${\mathcal F}_j^0$ the class of candidate regression functions for the $j$th predictor. More specifically, ${\mathcal F} _j^0=\{f(\cdot)={\mathbf h}_{\bolds\eta_j,j}(\bolds\eta_j^T\cdot)\bolds\xi, \sum_{i=1}^n f(\bolds\theta_{ij})=0, \bolds\eta_j\in\mathbb{R}^{q_n}, \bolds\xi\in\mathbb{R} ^{d_n}, \Vert \bolds\eta_j\Vert =1\}$.

nodes.name: Empirical l2 distance ||.||_n
nodes.statement: If~$\tilde f$ and~$\check{f}$ belong to~${\mathcal F}_j^0$, we denote by $\Vert \tilde f-\check{f}\Vert _n$ the $\ell_2$ distance between these two functions with respect to the empirical probability measure corresponding to $\bolds\theta_{1j},\ldots,\bolds\theta _{nj}$. More specifically, $\Vert \tilde f-\check{f}\Vert ^2_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (\tilde f(\bolds\theta_{ij})- \check{f}(\bolds\theta _{ij}))^2$.

nodes.name: Estimated regression function hat f_j
nodes.statement: We\vspace*{1pt} refer to the estimated regression function for the $j$th predictor as $\hat f_j(\cdot)=\hat g_j(\hat{\bolds\eta}_j^T\cdot)$.

nodes.name: True regression functions f_0j
nodes.statement: The\vspace*{1pt} corresponding true regression functions are referred to as $f_{0j}$.

nodes.name: Empirical distance between estimate and truth
nodes.statement: We slightly abuse the notation and write $\Vert \hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert _n$ for the $\ell_2$ distance between $\hat f_j$ and $f_{0j}$ with respect to the empirical probability measure corresponding to the $j$th predictor: \begin{eqnarray*} \Vert\hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert^2_n&=& \frac{1}n\sum_{i=1}^n \bigl[ \hat f_j(\bolds\theta_{ij})- f_{0j}(X_{ij}) \bigr]^2 \\ &=&\frac{1}n\sum_{i=1}^n \biggl[ \hat g_j \bigl(\hat{\bolds\eta}_j^T \bolds\theta_{ij} \bigr)- g_{0j} \biggl(\int_0^1 \beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt \biggr) \biggr]^2. \end{eqnarray*}

nodes.name: Signal index set (nonlinear setting)
nodes.statement: As before, we write~$\mathfrak{M}_0$ for the index set of the signal predictors, that is, $\mathfrak{M}_0 =\{j: 1\le j\le{p_n}, f_{0j}\ne0\}$.

nodes.name: Estimated index set
nodes.statement: We use~$\widehat {\mathfrak{M}}_n$ to denote the corresponding estimated set, $\{j: 1\le j\le {p_n}, \hat f_{j}\ne0\}$.

nodes.name: Universal constant
nodes.statement: A \textit{universal constant} is interpreted as a constant that does not depend on~$n$ or any of the other parameters that appear in the corresponding expression.
differentia: does not depend on~$n$ or any of the other parameters that appear in the corresponding expression

nodes.name: Asymptotic inequality notation
nodes.statement: Given expressions~$E_1$ and~$E_2$, we use~$E_1\gtrsim E_2$ to mean that there exists a positive universal constant~$c$, such that $E_1\ge cE_2$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic equivalence notation
nodes.statement: We write $E_1\asymp E_2$ when both $E_1\gtrsim E_2$ and $E_2\gtrsim E_1$ are satisfied.

nodes.name: Rate of convergence of nonlinear FAR
nodes.statement: Suppose that Conditions~\ref{cond3} and~\ref{as4} are satisfied. Let $q_n\gtrsim d_n\gtrsim\log\log n$. Then there exists a universal constant $c$, such that for $\lambda_n\ge c(n^{-1/2}q_n^{1/2}+n^{-1/2}\sqrt{\log{p_n}})$, the following bound holds with probability tending to one, as $n$ tends to infinity: \begin{equation} \sum_{j=1}^{{p_n}} \Vert \hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert_n= O \bigl(s_n\lambda_n+s_nd_n^{-2}+s_n^2n^{1/2}d_n^{-4}q_n^{-1/2} \bigr). \end{equation}
assumptions: Suppose that Conditions~\ref{cond3} and~\ref{as4} are satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: With $\ell_1$ penalty, the summed empirical $\ell_2$ errors of nonlinear FAR are $O(s_n\lambda_n+s_nd_n^{-2}+s_n^2n^{1/2}d_n^{-4}q_n^{-1/2})$.
nodes.label: nonlinthm

nodes.name: Nonlinear FAR error bound
nodes.statement: \sum_{j=1}^{{p_n}} \Vert \hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert_n= O \bigl(s_n\lambda_n+s_nd_n^{-2}+s_n^2n^{1/2}d_n^{-4}q_n^{-1/2} \bigr).
nodes.label: nonlinthmbnd

nodes.name: Optimal rate of nonlinear FAR
nodes.statement: Suppose that Conditions~\ref{cond3} and~\ref{as4} are satisfied. Let $q_n\asymp d_n\asymp(s_nn)^{1/5}$. Then\vspace*{1pt} there exists a universal constant $c$, such that for $\lambda_n \ge c(s_n^{1/10}n^{-2/5}+n^{-1/2}\sqrt{\log{p_n}})$, the following bound holds with probability tending to one, as $n$ tends to infinity: \[ \sum_{j=1}^{{p_n}} \Vert\hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert_n= O(s_n \lambda_n). \]
assumptions: Suppose that Conditions~\ref{cond3} and~\ref{as4} are satisfied.
nodes.label: nonlinratecor

nodes.name: Thresholded FAR estimator
nodes.statement: We define the thresholded FAR estimator as follows: $\tilde f_j=\hat f_j I{\{\Vert \hat f_j\Vert _n> \lambda_n\}}$, $j=1,\ldots ,p_n$.

nodes.name: Index set of thresholded estimator
nodes.statement: Let~$\widetilde{\mathfrak{M}}_n$ denote the index set of the corresponding nonzero regression function estimates, $\{j: 1\le j\le{p_n}, \tilde f_{j}\ne0\}$.

nodes.name: Error and model size bounds for thresholded FAR
nodes.statement: Under\vspace*{1pt} the assumptions of Corollary~\ref{nonlinratecor}, there exists a universal constant $c$, such that for $\lambda_n \ge c(s_n^{1/10}n^{-2/5}+n^{-1/2}\sqrt{\log{p_n}})$, the following bounds hold with probability tending to one, as $n$ tends to infinity: \begin{eqnarray*} \vert\widetilde{\mathfrak{M}}_n\vert &=& O(s_n)\quad \mbox{and} \\ \sum_{j=1}^{{p_n}} \Vert\tilde f_j-f_{0j}\Vert_n &=& O(s_n \lambda_n). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.label: threshthm

nodes.name: No false negatives and bounded false positives
nodes.statement: The estimation error bound in Theorem~\ref{threshthm} implies that, with probability tending to one, our estimator has zero false negatives, while the number of false positives stays bounded.
conclusions: our estimator has zero false negatives, while the number of false positives stays bounded

nodes.name: Exact support recovery by thresholded FAR
nodes.statement: Suppose that the components of the FAR model do not depend on~$n$. Suppose also that the assumptions of Corollary~\ref{nonlinratecor} are satisfied. Then there exist universal constants~$\tau_0$ and~$c$, such that, provided $\tau\ge\tau_0$, $\lambda_n \ge c(s_n^{1/10}n^{-2/5}+n^{-1/2}\sqrt{\log{p_n}})$ and $\lambda _n=o(1)$, we have \[ \widetilde{\mathfrak{M}}_n=\mathfrak{M}_0, \] with probability tending to one, as~$n$ goes to infinity.
assumptions: Suppose that the components of the FAR model do not depend on~$n$.
Suppose also that the assumptions of Corollary~\ref{nonlinratecor} are satisfied.
nodes.label: threshcor

nodes.name: Principal-component fallback initialization
nodes.statement: In the initialization step (step~0) of this algorithm, some of the $\bolds\eta_j$'s will likely be set to zero. This suggests that the corresponding predictors do not appear related to the response. However, the initialization assumes a linear model. It is conceivable that a response that appears unimportant using a linear model will become statistically significant using a nonlinear model. Hence, if $\bolds\eta_j$ is estimated to be zero in step~0 we instead set $\bolds\eta _j$ equal to the loading vector of the first principal component of $\Theta_j$. This estimate is the direction that explains the most variability in $X_{ij}(t)$ so is the most natural unsupervised projection and allows for potential nonlinear relationships to be detected in step~2.
nodes.section: A Details of the nonlinear FAR algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Indices set to zero by the linear initialization are replaced by the first principal component loading of $\Theta_j$.

nodes.name: Linearized index update (step 3 of nonlinear FAR)
nodes.statement: To implement step~3 of the FAR algorithm, we minimize (\ref{etaopt}) with respect to the $\bolds\eta_j$'s. Directly minimizing (\ref{etaopt}) is difficult due to the nonlinearity of the functions $g_j(t)\approx {\mathbf h}(t)^T\bolds\xi_j$. To overcome this difficulty, we observe that, with the estimate $\hat{\bolds\xi}_j$ from step~2 and the current value $\bolds\eta _{j,\mathrm{old}}$ of $\bolds\eta_j$, the first-order approximation of $g(\bolds\theta _{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j)\approx{\mathbf h}(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j$ is \begin{equation} \qquad{\mathbf h}\bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j \bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j\approx{\mathbf h}\bigl(\bolds\theta _{ij}^T\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}\bigr)^T \hat{\bolds\xi}_j + {\mathbf h}'\bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T \bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}\bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j \cdot \bolds\theta_{ij}^T(\bolds\eta_j-\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}). \end{equation} Thus, we can approximate (\ref{etaopt}) as \begin{equation} \sum_{i=1}^n \Biggl(R_i - \sum_{j=1}^p {\mathbf h}'\bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}} \bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j \cdot\bolds\theta_{ij}^T( \bolds\eta_j-\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}) \Biggr)^2, \end{equation} where\vspace*{1pt} $R_i = Y_i - \sum_{j=1}^p {\mathbf h}(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta _{j,\mathrm{old}})^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j $, that is, the residual for the $i$th observation from step~2 of the algorithm in the current iteration. The above approximation (\ref{etaoptapprox}) is a quadratic function of $\bolds\eta _j$ and can be minimized easily. Hence, the new value of $\bolds\eta_j$ is updated as the minimizer of (\ref{etaoptapprox}). We also note that if the estimate $\hat{\bolds\xi}_j$ from step~2 is $\mathbf{0}$, then the corresponding value of $\bolds\eta_j$ will not be updated.
nodes.section: A Details of the nonlinear FAR algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Update each index vector by minimizing a first-order Taylor linearization of the sum of squares, a quadratic in $\eta_j$.

nodes.name: First-order approximation of link
nodes.statement: \qquad{\mathbf h}\bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j \bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j\approx{\mathbf h}\bigl(\bolds\theta _{ij}^T\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}\bigr)^T \hat{\bolds\xi}_j + {\mathbf h}'\bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T \bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}\bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j \cdot \bolds\theta_{ij}^T(\bolds\eta_j-\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}).

nodes.name: Linearized sum of squares
nodes.statement: \sum_{i=1}^n \Biggl(R_i - \sum_{j=1}^p {\mathbf h}'\bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}} \bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j \cdot\bolds\theta_{ij}^T( \bolds\eta_j-\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}) \Biggr)^2,

nodes.label: etaoptapprox

nodes.name: Linearize link around current index
nodes.statement: To overcome this difficulty, we observe that, with the estimate $\hat{\bolds\xi}_j$ from step~2 and the current value $\bolds\eta _{j,\mathrm{old}}$ of $\bolds\eta_j$, the first-order approximation of $g(\bolds\theta _{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j)\approx{\mathbf h}(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j$ is \begin{equation} \qquad{\mathbf h}\bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j \bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j\approx{\mathbf h}\bigl(\bolds\theta _{ij}^T\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}\bigr)^T \hat{\bolds\xi}_j + {\mathbf h}'\bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T \bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}\bigr)^T\hat{\bolds\xi}_j \cdot \bolds\theta_{ij}^T(\bolds\eta_j-\bolds\eta_{j,\mathrm{old}}). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Penalty, signal strength and design conditions (Condition 2)
nodes.statement: (A) For any fixed $\lambda>0$, $\rho_{\lambda}(t)$ is concave and nondecreasing in $[0, \infty)$, and has nonincreasing first derivative $\rho_{\lambda}'(t)$. Further, $\rho'_\lambda(0+)>0$. (B) Let $a_n=\min_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0}\Vert \Theta_j\bolds\eta _{0,j}\Vert /\sqrt{n}$. It holds that $n^{\alpha} a_n \rightarrow\infty$ with $\alpha\in(0,\frac{1}{2})$. (C) It holds that $\rho'_{\lambda_n}(a_n/2)=o (n^{-\alpha }q_n^{-1}s_n^{-1/2} )$ and $\sup_{t\geq\sfrac{a_n}{2}}\rho ''_{\lambda_n}(t)=o(1)$. (D) There exists a positive constant $c_0$ such that \begin{equation} c_0\leq\min_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \Lambda_{\min}\biggl(\frac{1}{n} \Theta_{j}^T \Theta_{j}\biggr)<\Lambda_{\max}\biggl(\frac{1}{n} \Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^T\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}\biggr)\leq c_0^{-1}, \end{equation} where $\Lambda_{\min}$ and $\Lambda_{\max}$ are the smallest and largest eigenvalues of a matrix, respectively. Further, we have \begin{eqnarray} && \max_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \bigl\Vert\Theta_j \bigl(\Theta_j^T\Theta_j \bigr)^{-1}\Theta_j^T \Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0} \bigl(\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}^T\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0} \bigr)^{-1} \bigr\Vert_{\infty, 2}<\frac{\sqrt{c_0}}{2\sqrt{n}} \frac{\rho'_{\lambda_n}(0+)}{\rho '_{\lambda_n}(a_n/2)}, \end{eqnarray} where for a matrix $B$, $\Vert B\Vert _{\infty,2} = \sup _{\Vert {\mathbf x}\Vert _\infty=1}\Vert B{\mathbf x}\Vert _2$ with ${\mathbf x}$ a vector. (E) The model errors $\varepsilon_i$, $i=1,\ldots, n$ are independent and identically distributed as $N(0,\sigma^2)$.
nodes.label: as2

nodes.label: eqeigen

nodes.name: Discussion of Condition 2
nodes.statement: Condition~\ref{as2}(A) requires that the penalty functional, $\rho _{\lambda}(t)$, is concave and singular at 0. Many penalty functions proposed in the literature such as the hard thresholding penalty, SCAD \cite{fan2} and SICA \cite{lv1} all satisfy this condition. From (\ref{fexpan}), we see that Condition~\ref{as2}(B) places a lower bound on the signal strength of the true predictors $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$. In particular, it assumes that the weakest signal, $a_n$, can decay with sample size but the decay rate cannot be faster than $n^{-\alpha}$. Condition \ref{as2}(C) is a mild condition which can be easily satisfied by penalty functions with flat tails. For instance, if $\lambda_n = o(a_n/2)$, then for SCAD penalty, it can be verified from the definition that $\rho'_{\lambda_n}(a_n/2) = 0$ and $\rho''_{\lambda _n}(t) = 0$ for all $t \geq a_n/2$, and thus\vspace*{1pt} Condition~\ref{as2}(C) is satisfied. Although Condition~\ref{as2}(C) assumes the existence of the second-order derivative for $\rho_{\lambda_n}(t)$, it can be relaxed to the existence of the first-order derivative by using the local concavity definition in \cite {lv1}. Condition~\ref{as2}(D) relates to the design matrix for the signal predictors, $\Theta _{\mathfrak{M}_0}$. We assume that the eigenvalues for the design matrix corresponding to true predictors are bounded from below and above. If $\Theta_{\mathfrak{M}_0}$ is orthogonal, then (\ref{eqeigen}) is satisfied with $c_0 = 1$. The upper bound in condition (\ref{e015}) depends on the penalty function through the ratio $\rho'_{\lambda_n}(0+)/\rho_{\lambda_n}'(a_n/2)$, which is larger than 1 for concave penalties and equal to 1 for the group Lasso penalty, $\rho_{\lambda_n}(t)=\lambda_n t$. For instance, if $\lambda_n = o(a_n)$, then $\rho'_{\lambda_n}(0+)/\rho_{\lambda_n}'(a_n/2) = \infty$ for SCAD penalty and thus (\ref{e015}) is satisfied automatically.
nodes.statement_short: Hard thresholding, SCAD and SICA satisfy the penalty conditions; orthogonal designs satisfy the eigenvalue bound.

nodes.name: Truncated true index vector eta_j^*
nodes.statement: Given an orthonormal basis expansion for $\beta_j(t)$, that is, $\beta _j(t)=\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}\eta^*_{jl}b_l(t)$, we will define $\bolds\eta _j^*=(\eta^*_{j1},\ldots,\eta^*_{jq_n})^T$.

nodes.name: Best spline approximation f_j^*
nodes.statement: We will also define $f_j^*(\bolds\theta_{ij})={\mathbf h}_{\bolds\eta^*_j,j}(\bolds\theta _{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*)\bolds\xi^*$, where $\bolds\xi_j^*$ is chosen to minimize $\sum_{i=1}^n [{\mathbf h}_{\bolds\eta^*_j,j}\times\break (\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*)\bolds\xi -g_{0j}(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*)]^2$ over~$\bolds\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d_n}$ with the constraint $\sum_i f_j^*(\bolds\theta_{ij})=0$.

nodes.name: Regularity conditions for nonlinear FAR (Condition 3)
nodes.statement: (A) Functional predictors, $\{X_{ij}:[0,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, i=1,\ldots,n, j=1,\ldots,{p_n}\}$, belong\vspace*{1pt} to a Sobolev ellipsoid of order two: there exists a universal constant $C$, such that $\sum _{k=1}^{\infty} \theta^2_{ijk}k^4\le C^2$ for all $i=1,\ldots,n, j=1,\ldots,{p_n}$. (B) The true index functions, $\{\beta_j(t), j\in\mathfrak{M}_0\} $, satisfy $\int_0^1\beta^2_j(t)\,dt=1$. (C) Errors~$\varepsilon_i$ are independent and uniformly sub-Gaussian. (D) The true link functions, $g_{0j}$, are twice continuously differentiable and are bounded, together with their first and second derivatives, uniformly over~$j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$ and~$n$. (E) For\vspace*{1pt} each $\bolds\eta$ with $\Vert \bolds\eta\Vert =1$ and each $j\le {p_n}$ let~$Q_{\bolds\eta,j,n}$ denote the empirical distribution associated with the index values $\bolds\eta^T\bolds\theta_{1j},\ldots, \bolds\eta^T\bolds\theta_{nj}$. Assume that there exist corresponding probability distributions~$P_{\bolds\eta,j,n}$, each with bounded support and a positive continuous density, such that the densities are bounded both above and away from zero uniformly over $j$ and $n$, and \begin{equation} \sup_{u\in\mathbb{R}, \Vert \bolds\eta\Vert =1, 1\le j\le{p_n}}\bigl\vert Q_{\bolds\eta ,j,n}(- \infty,u]-P_{\bolds\eta,j,n}(-\infty,u]\bigr\vert=o \bigl(d_n^{-1} \bigr). \end{equation}
nodes.label: cond3

nodes.name: Uniform approximation of index distributions
nodes.statement: \sup_{u\in\mathbb{R}, \Vert \bolds\eta\Vert =1, 1\le j\le{p_n}}\bigl\vert Q_{\bolds\eta ,j,n}(- \infty,u]-P_{\bolds\eta,j,n}(-\infty,u]\bigr\vert=o \bigl(d_n^{-1} \bigr).

nodes.name: Discussion of Condition 3
nodes.statement: Condition~\ref{cond3}(A) is identical to Condition~\ref{as3}(A), imposed for the linear FAR theory. It is a common smoothness requirement in nonparametric regression, when the orthogonal basis approach is used, as discussed, for example, in Chapter~8 in \cite {Bwasserman1}. Condition~\ref{cond3}(B) is imposed for identifiability. Conditions~\ref{cond3}(C) and~(D) are typical in high-dimensional regression and nonparametric regression problems, respectively. The reason we require uniformity is to handle the situation where the number of signal predictors grows with~$n$. Again, uniformity is needed to handle the growing number of signal predictors.\vspace*{1pt} Condition~\ref{cond3}(E) ensures that the candidate index values, $\bolds\eta^T\bolds\theta_{1j},\ldots, \bolds\eta^T\bolds\theta_{nj}$, have sufficiently regular distributions. Assumptions of this form are typical in spline estimation \cite{zhou2}, for example.

nodes.name: Discussion of Condition 4
nodes.statement: Condition~\ref{as4}(A) is a natural generalization of the \emph{compatibility condition} used in high-dimensional additive models, for example, in \cite{meier1} and Section~8.4. in \cite{Bbuhlmann1}. Note that because we do not use a smoothness penalty in our estimation approach, the smoothness penalty does not appear in the compatibility condition. Condition~\ref{as4}(B) is a version of the standard regularity condition on the behavior of the sum of squares function near its minimum. Assumptions of this form have been imposed in the single index model literature, for example, \cite{yu1}. We again require uniformity over $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$ to handle the growing number of signal predictors.

nodes.name: Compatibility and index regularity conditions (Condition 4)
nodes.statement: (A) There exists a positive universal constant $\phi^2$ for which the following holds. If functions $\{h_j, j=1,\ldots,{p_n}\}$ are such that each $h_j$ is a difference of two functions in ${\mathcal F}_j^0$, and inequality $\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c}\Vert h_{j}\Vert _n\le3\sum _{j\in \mathfrak{M}_0}\Vert h_{j}\Vert _n$ is satisfied, then the following inequality holds: $\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0}\Vert h_{j}\Vert _n^2\le\Vert \sum _{j=1}^{{p_n}}h_j\Vert ^2_n/\phi^2$. (B) There exist positive universal constants $\tau$, $c_1$ and $c_2$, such that for all sufficiently large~$n$ and each $f_{\bolds\eta _j,j}(\cdot)={\mathbf h}_{\bolds\eta_j,j}(\bolds\eta_j^T\cdot)\bolds\xi$ with~$\Vert \bolds\eta_j\Vert =\Vert \bolds\eta_j^*\Vert $ and $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$, inequalities $\Vert f_{\bolds\eta_j,j} - f^*_j\Vert _n\le\tau$ and $\Vert \bolds\eta_j-\bolds\eta _j^*\Vert <\Vert \bolds\eta_j+\bolds\eta_j^*\Vert $ imply $\Vert \bolds\eta_j-\bolds\eta _j^*\Vert \le c_1\Vert f_{\bolds\eta_j,j} - f^*_j\Vert _n$ and $\Vert f_{\bolds\eta_j^*,j} - f^*_j\Vert _n\le c_2\Vert f_{\bolds\eta_j,j} - f^*_j\Vert _n$.
nodes.label: as4

nodes.name: Derivation of approximation error bound
nodes.statement: We start by deriving a bound on the error due to our approximation of index functions~$\beta_j$ and link functions~$g_{0j}$. Observe that \begin{eqnarray*} \biggl\vert\int_0^1\beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt - \bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*\biggr\vert ^2&=&\Biggl\vert\sum_{k=q_n+1}^{\infty} \eta^*_{jk}k^{-2}k^2\theta_{ijk}\Biggr \vert^2 \\ &\le&\sum_{k=q_n+1}^{\infty}\bigl( \eta^*_{jk}\bigr)^2k^{-4}\sum _{k=q_n+1}^{\infty}\theta^2_{ijk}k^{-4}. \end{eqnarray*} Condition~\ref{cond3}(A) implies that the right-most sum is bounded by a universal constant~$C^2$. Also\vspace*{1pt} note that $\sum_{l=q_n+1}^{\infty }(\eta_{jl}^*)^2k^{-4}\le q_n^{-4}\sum_{k=q_n+1}^{\infty}(\eta _{jk}^*)^2\le q_n^{-4}$, by Condition~\ref{cond3}(B). Thus, if we set $I_{ij}=\int_0^1\beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt$, then the bound $\vert I_{ij} - \bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*\vert \le Cq_n^{-2}$ holds for all $n$, $i$, and $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$. Hence, if we let $\widetilde C$ be the uniform bound over the first derivatives in Condition~\ref{cond3}(D), then \begin{equation} \bigl\vert g_{0j}(I_{ij}) - g_{0j} \bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^* \bigr)\bigr\vert\le\widetilde C\bigl\vert I_{ij} - \bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*\bigr\vert= O \bigl(q_n^{-2}\bigr), \end{equation} uniformly over $i$ and $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$. Set $M_j=\sup_t\vert g^{\prime \prime}_{0j}(t)\vert $ for $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$, and note that constants $M_j$ are uniformly bounded by Condition~\ref{cond3}(D). Taking advantage of the approximation bounds for the cubic B-splines (e.g., Corollary~6.21 in \cite{BSchumaker1}), we then have \begin{equation} n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \bigl(g_{0j} \bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T \bolds\eta_j^* \bigr)-f^*_j(\bolds\theta_{ij}) \bigr)^2=O\bigl(d_n^{-4}M_j^2 \bigr)=O\bigl(d_n^{-4}\bigr), \end{equation} uniformly over $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$. Combining inequalities~(\ref {prelimappr1}) and~(\ref{prelimappr2}), we deduce $\Vert f_{0j}-f_{j}^*\Vert _n=O(q_n^{-2}+d_n^{-2})=O(d_n^{-2})$, uniformly over $j$. Note that for $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c$, both $f_{0j}$ and $f_{j}^*$ are zero.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz with Sobolev decay bounds index error, Lipschitz links transfer it, and B-spline approximation bounds handle link error.

nodes.name: Index approximation transfer bound
nodes.statement: \bigl\vert g_{0j}(I_{ij}) - g_{0j} \bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^* \bigr)\bigr\vert\le\widetilde C\bigl\vert I_{ij} - \bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*\bigr\vert= O \bigl(q_n^{-2}\bigr),

nodes.name: B-spline approximation bound
nodes.statement: n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \bigl(g_{0j} \bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T \bolds\eta_j^* \bigr)-f^*_j(\bolds\theta_{ij}) \bigr)^2=O\bigl(d_n^{-4}M_j^2 \bigr)=O\bigl(d_n^{-4}\bigr),
nodes.label: prelimappr2

nodes.name: Goal: approximation error bound
nodes.statement: We start by deriving a bound on the error due to our approximation of index functions~$\beta_j$ and link functions~$g_{0j}$.
nodes.statement_short: State the aim: bound index and link approximation errors.

nodes.name: Bound index approximation error
nodes.statement: Observe that \begin{eqnarray*} \biggl\vert\int_0^1\beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt - \bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*\biggr\vert ^2&=&\Biggl\vert\sum_{k=q_n+1}^{\infty} \eta^*_{jk}k^{-2}k^2\theta_{ijk}\Biggr \vert^2 \\ &\le&\sum_{k=q_n+1}^{\infty}\bigl( \eta^*_{jk}\bigr)^2k^{-4}\sum _{k=q_n+1}^{\infty}\theta^2_{ijk}k^{-4}. \end{eqnarray*} Condition~\ref{cond3}(A) implies that the right-most sum is bounded by a universal constant~$C^2$. Also\vspace*{1pt} note that $\sum_{l=q_n+1}^{\infty }(\eta_{jl}^*)^2k^{-4}\le q_n^{-4}\sum_{k=q_n+1}^{\infty}(\eta _{jk}^*)^2\le q_n^{-4}$, by Condition~\ref{cond3}(B). Thus, if we set $I_{ij}=\int_0^1\beta_j(t)X_{ij}(t)\,dt$, then the bound $\vert I_{ij} - \bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*\vert \le Cq_n^{-2}$ holds for all $n$, $i$, and $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz and Condition 3(A),(B) give $|I_{ij}-\theta_{ij}^T\eta_j^*|\le Cq_n^{-2}$.

nodes.name: Transfer through link
nodes.statement: Hence, if we let $\widetilde C$ be the uniform bound over the first derivatives in Condition~\ref{cond3}(D), then \begin{equation} \bigl\vert g_{0j}(I_{ij}) - g_{0j} \bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^* \bigr)\bigr\vert\le\widetilde C\bigl\vert I_{ij} - \bolds\theta_{ij}^T\bolds\eta_j^*\bigr\vert= O \bigl(q_n^{-2}\bigr), \end{equation} uniformly over $i$ and $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Bounded derivative of $g_{0j}$ transfers the bound to $O(q_n^{-2})$.

nodes.name: B-spline approximation bound
nodes.statement: Set $M_j=\sup_t\vert g^{\prime \prime}_{0j}(t)\vert $ for $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$, and note that constants $M_j$ are uniformly bounded by Condition~\ref{cond3}(D). Taking advantage of the approximation bounds for the cubic B-splines (e.g., Corollary~6.21 in \cite{BSchumaker1}), we then have \begin{equation} n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \bigl(g_{0j} \bigl(\bolds\theta_{ij}^T \bolds\eta_j^* \bigr)-f^*_j(\bolds\theta_{ij}) \bigr)^2=O\bigl(d_n^{-4}M_j^2 \bigr)=O\bigl(d_n^{-4}\bigr), \end{equation} uniformly over $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply cubic B-spline approximation bounds to get $O(d_n^{-4})$.

nodes.name: Combine bounds
nodes.statement: Combining inequalities~(\ref {prelimappr1}) and~(\ref{prelimappr2}), we deduce $\Vert f_{0j}-f_{j}^*\Vert _n=O(q_n^{-2}+d_n^{-2})=O(d_n^{-2})$, uniformly over $j$. Note that for $j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c$, both $f_{0j}$ and $f_{j}^*$ are zero.
nodes.statement_short: Combine to get $\|f_{0j}-f_j^*\|_n=O(d_n^{-2})$, zero for noise predictors.

nodes.name: Summed approximation error bound
nodes.statement: Consequently, \begin{equation} \sum_{j=1}^{{p_n}}\bigl\Vert f_j^*-f_{0j}\bigr\Vert_n=O \bigl(s_nd_n^{-2}\bigr). \end{equation}

nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.statement_short: Basic inequality from the penalized fit plus the empirical process lemma, then two cases. In the main case a cone condition allows the compatibility condition to give the $O(s_n\lambda_n)$ rate.

nodes.name: Basic identity
nodes.statement: \Vert y-\hat f\Vert_n^2-\bigl \Vert y-f^*\bigr\Vert_n^2=\Vert\hat f-f_0\Vert_n^2-\bigl\Vert f^*-f_0\bigr\Vert_n^2-2\bigl(\varepsilon, \hat f - f^*\bigr)_n.
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.label: basicineq1

nodes.name: Basic inequality with lemma
nodes.statement: && \Vert\hat f-f_0\Vert_n^2+ \lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n}\Vert \hat f_j\Vert_n \nonumber\\[-10pt]\\[-10pt]\nonumber &&\qquad \le e_n^2+2C_1s_nr_n^2+2C_1r_n \sum_{j=1}^{p_n}\bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n+ \lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n}\bigl \Vert f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n,

nodes.label: basicineq1b

nodes.name: Simplified inequality on case (ii) event
nodes.statement: && \bigl\Vert\hat f-f^*\bigr\Vert_n^2+2 \lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j\Vert_n \nonumber\\[-8pt]\\[-8pt]\nonumber &&\qquad \le4(C_1+1)r_n \sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n+2\lambda _n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n.

nodes.name: Stochastic bound in lambda

nodes.label: stochbndlam

nodes.name: Cone condition
nodes.statement: \sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n\le3\sum _{j\in \mathfrak{M}_0} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^* \bigr\Vert_n.

nodes.label: compatbnd

nodes.name: Notation and basic identity
nodes.statement: Let $\Vert y-f\Vert ^2_n$ denote $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-f(\bolds\theta _{i}))^2$ and let $\Vert f\Vert ^2_n$ denote $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f(\bolds\theta_{i})^2$. Consider the following simple identity: \begin{equation} \Vert y-\hat f\Vert_n^2-\bigl \Vert y-f^*\bigr\Vert_n^2=\Vert\hat f-f_0\Vert_n^2-\bigl\Vert f^*-f_0\bigr\Vert_n^2-2\bigl(\varepsilon, \hat f - f^*\bigr)_n. \end{equation}
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.statement_short: Introduce empirical norms and the basic least-squares identity.

nodes.name: Basic inequality
nodes.statement: Note that $\Vert y-\hat f\Vert _n^2+\lambda_n\sum _{j=1}^{p_n}\Vert \hat f_j\Vert _n-\Vert y-f^*\Vert _n^2-\lambda_n\sum _{j=1}^{p_n}\Vert f_j^*\Vert _n\le0$ by the definition of~$\hat f$. Let~$e_n$ denote the approximation error, $\Vert f^* - f_0\Vert _n$. Inequality~(\ref{basicineq1}) then implies \[ \Vert\hat f-f_0\Vert_n^2+ \lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n}\Vert \hat f_j\Vert_n\le e_n^2+2 \bigl(\varepsilon,\hat f - f^*\bigr)_n+\lambda_n\sum _{j=1}^{p_n}\bigl\Vert f_j^* \bigr\Vert_n. \]
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.statement_short: Optimality of $\hat f$ turns the identity into a basic inequality.

nodes.name: Apply empirical process lemma
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lementrcons}, the above inequality yields \begin{eqnarray} && \Vert\hat f-f_0\Vert_n^2+ \lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n}\Vert \hat f_j\Vert_n \nonumber\\[-10pt]\\[-10pt]\nonumber &&\qquad \le e_n^2+2C_1s_nr_n^2+2C_1r_n \sum_{j=1}^{p_n}\bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n+ \lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n}\bigl \Vert f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n, \end{eqnarray} with probability tending to one.
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.statement_short: Bound the noise cross term by Lemma 1.

nodes.name: Case (i)
nodes.statement: [\textit{Case} (i).] Consider the event $e_n^2+C_1s_nr_n^2\ge r_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f_j^*\Vert _n$. Note that $e_n^2=O(s_n^2d_n^{-4})$ by~(\ref{approxbnd}). Thus, $\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f_j^*\Vert _n = O(s_n^2n^{1/2}d_n^{-4}\*q_n^{-1/2}+s_nr_n)$. Consequently, $\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert _n=O(d_n^{-4}q_n^{-1/2}+s_nr_n+s_nd_n^{-2})$, which implies the stochastic bound in display~(\ref{nonlinthmbnd}).
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.statement_short: When approximation error dominates, the bound follows directly.

nodes.name: Case (ii)
nodes.statement: [\textit{Case} (ii).] Consider the event $e_n^2+C_1s_nr_n^2< r_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f_j^*\Vert _n$.\vadjust{\goodbreak} Using inequality $\Vert \hat f-f^*\Vert ^2_n\le 2\Vert \hat f-f_0\Vert _n^2 +2e_n^2$ together with~(\ref{basicineq1b}), we get \begin{eqnarray*} && \bigl\Vert\hat f-f^*\bigr\Vert_n^2+2 \lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j\Vert_n \\ &&\qquad \le4e_n^2+4C_1s_nr_n^2+4C_1r_n \sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n+2 \lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl \Vert f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n. \end{eqnarray*} On the event $e_n^2+C_1s_nr_n^2< r_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f_j^*\Vert _n$ the above inequality simplifies to \begin{eqnarray} && \bigl\Vert\hat f-f^*\bigr\Vert_n^2+2 \lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j\Vert_n \nonumber\\[-8pt]\\[-8pt]\nonumber &&\qquad \le4(C_1+1)r_n \sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n+2\lambda _n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n. \end{eqnarray} Because we assume $r_n=O(\lambda_n)$, we can rewrite inequality~(\ref {basicineq3}) as \begin{equation} \bigl\Vert\hat f-f^*\bigr\Vert_n^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f^*_j\bigr\Vert_n O( \lambda_n). \end{equation} Inequality~(\ref{basicineq3}) also gives \[ \sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \Vert\hat f_j\Vert _n\le2\lambda_n^{-1}(C_1+1)r_n \sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n+\sum _{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^* \bigr\Vert_n. \] Consequently, \begin{eqnarray*} \sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n &\le& 2\lambda _n^{-1}(C_1+1)r_n\sum _{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^* \bigr\Vert_n \\ &&{} +\bigl[2\lambda_n^{-1}(C_1+1)r_n+1 \bigr]\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n, \end{eqnarray*} which, provided $\lambda_n\ge4(C_1+1)r_n$, implies \begin{equation} \sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n\le3\sum _{j\in \mathfrak{M}_0} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^* \bigr\Vert_n. \end{equation} This allows us to apply the compatibility condition,~\ref{as4}(A), to $\hat f -f^*$. It follows that $s_n^{-1}(\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \Vert \hat f_j-f^*_j\Vert _n)^2\le\Vert \hat f-f^*\Vert _n^2/\phi^2$, which, by~(\ref{compatbnd}), yields $s_n^{-1}(\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f^*_j\Vert _n)^2\le16\Vert \hat f-f^*\Vert _n^2/\phi ^2$. Stochastic bound~(\ref{stochbndlam}) then gives $\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f^*_j\Vert _n= O(s_n\lambda_n)$, and\vspace*{2pt} hence $\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert _n= O(s_n\lambda_n+s_nd_n^{-2})$, which again implies the bound in display~(\ref{nonlinthmbnd}). This completes the proof of Theorem~\ref{nonlinthm}.
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.statement_short: When the estimation error dominates, derive a cone condition and apply compatibility.

nodes.name: Squared error inequality
nodes.statement: Using inequality $\Vert \hat f-f^*\Vert ^2_n\le 2\Vert \hat f-f_0\Vert _n^2 +2e_n^2$ together with~(\ref{basicineq1b}), we get \begin{eqnarray*} && \bigl\Vert\hat f-f^*\bigr\Vert_n^2+2 \lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j\Vert_n \\ &&\qquad \le4e_n^2+4C_1s_nr_n^2+4C_1r_n \sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n+2 \lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl \Vert f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.statement_short: Combine with $\|\hat f-f^*\|^2\le 2\|\hat f-f_0\|^2+2e_n^2$.

nodes.name: Simplify on event
nodes.statement: On the event $e_n^2+C_1s_nr_n^2< r_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f_j^*\Vert _n$ the above inequality simplifies to \begin{eqnarray} && \bigl\Vert\hat f-f^*\bigr\Vert_n^2+2 \lambda_n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j\Vert_n \nonumber\\[-8pt]\\[-8pt]\nonumber &&\qquad \le4(C_1+1)r_n \sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n+2\lambda _n\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.statement_short: Absorb approximation terms on the case (ii) event.

nodes.name: Stochastic bound
nodes.statement: Because we assume $r_n=O(\lambda_n)$, we can rewrite inequality~(\ref {basicineq3}) as \begin{equation} \bigl\Vert\hat f-f^*\bigr\Vert_n^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f^*_j\bigr\Vert_n O( \lambda_n). \end{equation}
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.statement_short: Use $r_n=O(\lambda_n)$ to get the stochastic bound.

nodes.name: Cone condition
nodes.statement: Inequality~(\ref{basicineq3}) also gives \[ \sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \Vert\hat f_j\Vert _n\le2\lambda_n^{-1}(C_1+1)r_n \sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j - f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n+\sum _{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^* \bigr\Vert_n. \] Consequently, \begin{eqnarray*} \sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n &\le& 2\lambda _n^{-1}(C_1+1)r_n\sum _{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^* \bigr\Vert_n \\ &&{} +\bigl[2\lambda_n^{-1}(C_1+1)r_n+1 \bigr]\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n, \end{eqnarray*} which, provided $\lambda_n\ge4(C_1+1)r_n$, implies \begin{equation} \sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^*\bigr\Vert_n\le3\sum _{j\in \mathfrak{M}_0} \bigl\Vert\hat f_j-f_j^* \bigr\Vert_n. \end{equation}
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.statement_short: Derive the cone condition (compatbnd) for $\lambda_n\ge 4(C_1+1)r_n$.

nodes.name: Apply compatibility and conclude
nodes.statement: This allows us to apply the compatibility condition,~\ref{as4}(A), to $\hat f -f^*$. It follows that $s_n^{-1}(\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \Vert \hat f_j-f^*_j\Vert _n)^2\le\Vert \hat f-f^*\Vert _n^2/\phi^2$, which, by~(\ref{compatbnd}), yields $s_n^{-1}(\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f^*_j\Vert _n)^2\le16\Vert \hat f-f^*\Vert _n^2/\phi ^2$. Stochastic bound~(\ref{stochbndlam}) then gives $\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f^*_j\Vert _n= O(s_n\lambda_n)$, and\vspace*{2pt} hence $\sum_{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert _n= O(s_n\lambda_n+s_nd_n^{-2})$, which again implies the bound in display~(\ref{nonlinthmbnd}). This completes the proof of Theorem~\ref{nonlinthm}.
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.statement_short: Compatibility condition and the stochastic bound give $O(s_n\lambda_n)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{threshthm}, the error bound in the statement of Theorem~\ref{nonlinthm} simplifies to $\sum _{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert _n=O(s_n\lambda_n)$. Consequently, on the sets of probability tending to one, \begin{equation} \sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \Vert\tilde f_j\Vert_n\le\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M} _0^c} \Vert\hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert_n=O(s_n \lambda_n). \end{equation} Using bound~(\ref{bndprfthrthm}) and the fact that $\Vert \tilde f_j\Vert _n>\lambda_n$ for $j\in\widetilde{\mathfrak{M}}_n$, we can deduce $\vert \mathfrak{M}_0^c\cap\widetilde{\mathfrak{M}}_n\vert =O(s_n)$. This implies $\vert \widetilde{\mathfrak{M}}_n\vert \le\vert \mathfrak{M}_0\vert +\vert \mathfrak{M}_0^c\cap\widetilde {\mathfrak{M}}_n\vert =O(s_n)$. Also note that \[ \sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \Vert\tilde f_j-f_{0j} \Vert_n\le\sum_{j\in \mathfrak{M}_0}\bigl( \lambda_n+ \Vert\hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert _n\bigr) =O(s_n\lambda_n). \] The above bound, together with~(\ref{bndprfthrthm}), yields the error bound in Theorem~\ref{threshthm}.
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.statement_short: Use Theorem 3's $O(s_n\lambda_n)$ bound: thresholded noise components are few, and thresholding adds at most $\lambda_n$ per signal component.

nodes.name: Noise component bound after thresholding
nodes.statement: \sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \Vert\tilde f_j\Vert_n\le\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M} _0^c} \Vert\hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert_n=O(s_n \lambda_n).
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.label: bndprfthrthm

nodes.name: Bound noise components
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{threshthm}, the error bound in the statement of Theorem~\ref{nonlinthm} simplifies to $\sum _{j=1}^{p_n} \Vert \hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert _n=O(s_n\lambda_n)$. Consequently, on the sets of probability tending to one, \begin{equation} \sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0^c} \Vert\tilde f_j\Vert_n\le\sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M} _0^c} \Vert\hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert_n=O(s_n \lambda_n). \end{equation}
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.statement_short: Specialize Theorem 3 and bound the thresholded noise components.

nodes.name: Bound model size
nodes.statement: Using bound~(\ref{bndprfthrthm}) and the fact that $\Vert \tilde f_j\Vert _n>\lambda_n$ for $j\in\widetilde{\mathfrak{M}}_n$, we can deduce $\vert \mathfrak{M}_0^c\cap\widetilde{\mathfrak{M}}_n\vert =O(s_n)$. This implies $\vert \widetilde{\mathfrak{M}}_n\vert \le\vert \mathfrak{M}_0\vert +\vert \mathfrak{M}_0^c\cap\widetilde {\mathfrak{M}}_n\vert =O(s_n)$.
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.statement_short: Threshold $\lambda_n$ implies $O(s_n)$ selected predictors.

nodes.name: Bound signal error and conclude
nodes.statement: Also note that \[ \sum_{j\in\mathfrak{M}_0} \Vert\tilde f_j-f_{0j} \Vert_n\le\sum_{j\in \mathfrak{M}_0}\bigl( \lambda_n+ \Vert\hat f_j-f_{0j}\Vert _n\bigr) =O(s_n\lambda_n). \] The above bound, together with~(\ref{bndprfthrthm}), yields the error bound in Theorem~\ref{threshthm}.
nodes.section: C.3 Main body of the proof
nodes.statement_short: Signal components incur at most $\lambda_n$ extra error each.
